title: How to find out who is behind a fake account
summary: Attribution from public evidence means building links between an account and a known identity and saying how strong each one is.
body_markdown:
Build links from the account to a known identity using public evidence, and say how strong each one is. Check what the account shows about itself, search its photos and handle elsewhere, research any website, email address or phone number it published, and look for sibling accounts in the same campaign. Public evidence can often tie an account to its operator's other accounts and handles, while naming the person usually takes the platform, which holds the account's registration and log-in data.


Sometimes, from what the operator reused: a rare handle used for years elsewhere, a website or email address they control, or a photo or page template shared with other accounts. Each link needs a date and a source, and a name needs a link that does not rest on anything the operator wrote. When public evidence runs out, report the account to the platform, which holds its registration and log-in data.


It tells you where the photo came from, which is evidence about the account, and it says something about the operator only when the same image appears on other accounts. A match on older pages under another name means the photo was very likely taken from someone else, who is usually a victim. No match settles nothing, because it fits a real person whose photo is not posted elsewhere and a generated face equally well.


No. Messaging, following or trying to trick the account tells the operator someone is looking, which can lead them to delete accounts or change handles before you finish, and drawing information out of someone under a false identity takes the work outside open-source research. Leave password reset and account recovery forms alone for the same reason. Save your evidence and report the account instead.


Look for specific overlaps: the same images, bio or post text, creation dates in a short window, the same followers, and links to domains registered together or built from one template. Weigh each overlap by how many unrelated accounts could share it by chance, and count two overlaps that come from one fact as one. Several specific, independent links make a shared operator likely.


Use the platform's own impersonation report and attach the evidence you saved, with addresses and capture times. Facebook accepts impersonation reports even from people without an account, and X has a report for an account posing as you or your brand. Instagram lets you report an account in the app for pretending to be you, someone you follow, a public figure or a business, and asks the person impersonated for a photo of a government-issued ID. If anyone is in immediate danger call 911, report threats to the FBI or local police, and report scams or extortion to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center.
